{{short description|Theorem on powers of primes dividing binomial coefficients}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Kummer's theorem''' is a formula for the exponent of the highest power of a [[prime number]] ''p'' that divides a given binomial coefficient.  In other words, it gives the [[p-adic valuation|''p''-adic valuation]] of a [[binomial coefficient]]. The theorem is named after [[Ernst Kummer]], who proved it in 1852 {{harv|Kummer|1852}}.

==Statement==
Kummer's theorem states that for given [[integer]]s ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;''m''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0 and a prime number ''p'', the ''p''-adic valuation <math>\nu_p\!\tbinom n m </math> of the binomial coefficient <math>\tbinom{n}{m}</math> is equal to the number of [[carry (arithmetic)|carries]] when ''m'' is added to ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''m'' in [[radix|base]]&nbsp;''p''.

An equivalent formation of the theorem is as follows:

Write the base-<math>p</math> expansion of the integer <math>n</math> as <math>n=n_0+n_1p+n_2p^2+\cdots+n_rp^r</math>, and define <math>S_p(n):=n_0+n_1+\cdots+n_r</math> to be the sum of the base-<math>p</math> digits. Then
: <math>\nu_p\!\binom nm  = \dfrac{S_p(m) + S_p(n-m) - S_p(n)}{p-1}.</math>

The theorem can be proved by writing <math>\tbinom{n}{m}</math> as <math>\tfrac{n!}{m! (n-m)!}</math> and using [[Legendre's formula]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Mihet|first=Dorel|date=December 2010|title=Legendre's and Kummer's Theorems Again|url=https://www.ias.ac.in/article/fulltext/reso/015/12/1111-1121|journal=Resonance|volume=15|issue=12|pages=1111–1121|doi=10.1007/s12045-010-0123-4 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== Examples ===

To compute the largest power of 2 dividing the binomial coefficient <math>\tbinom{10}{3} </math> write {{math| ''m'' {{=}} 3}} and {{math| ''n'' − ''m'' {{=}} 7}} in base {{math| ''p'' {{=}} 2}} as {{math|3 {{=}} 11<sub>2</sub>}} and {{math|7 {{=}} 111<sub>2</sub>}}.  Carrying out the addition {{math| 11<sub>2</sub> + 111<sub>2</sub> {{=}} 1010<sub>2</sub>}} in base 2 requires three carries:
: <math>\begin{array}{ccccc}
& _1 & _1 & _1 \\
& & & 1 & 1 \,_2 \\
+ & & 1 & 1 & 1 \,_2 \\\hline
& 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \,_2
\end{array}</math>
Therefore the largest power of 2 that divides <math>\tbinom{10}{3} = 120 = 2^3 \cdot 15 </math> is 3.

Alternatively, the form involving sums of digits can be used. The sums of digits of 3, 7, and 10 in base 2 are <math> S_2(3) = 1 + 1 = 2</math>, <math> S_2(7) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3</math>, and <math> S_2(10) = 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 2</math> respectively. Then
: <math>\nu_2\!\binom {10}3  = \dfrac{S_2(3) + S_2(7) - S_2(10)}{2 - 1} = \dfrac{2 + 3 - 2}{2 - 1} = 3.</math>

==Multinomial coefficient generalization==
Kummer's theorem can be generalized to [[multinomial coefficient]]s <math> \tbinom n {m_1,\ldots,m_k} = \tfrac{n!}{m_1!\cdots m_k!}</math> as follows: 

: <math>\nu_p\!\binom n {m_1,\ldots,m_k} = \dfrac{1}{p-1} \left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^k S_p(m_i) \right) - S_p(n) \right).</math>
